lessons.title: Examples can miss a bug
lessons.slogan: A few answers are not a rule.
lessons.vision: Arrange four seats in every row of a small event hall. You will turn a couple of examples into a rule for every row count in a stated domain.
lessons.explanation: In F#, let names a value or function. In seats (rows: int) : int, rows is an integer input and the final int is the result type. Indentation groups the branches. The = in a test compares values; it does not change them. A LawSpec arrow describes input and output types. Its for all introduces a rule over the stated inputs. In Tests.fs, [| ... |] builds an array of checks. A comma pairs a name such as "one row" with a true/false observation. The () in examples () means the function needs no input. module groups a file's names; open Solution makes seats available in Tests.fs.
lessons.news: The supplied code memorizes two examples. A property describes a relationship between inputs and outputs, so new inputs can expose that shortcut.
lessons.contributions: Your seat function, an extra example and an unchanged general property. Passing runs support the checked row counts 0–40, under the browser adapter; they do not prove all integer arithmetic.

star.salient: A function can agree with examples while violating the intended rule.
star.slogan: A few answers are not a rule.
star.symbol: The visible table leaves a question mark at row 3; executing that row fills the gap.
star.surprise: Both original tests pass even though almost every other row count is wrong.
star.story: An event organizer adds a third row; the memorized estimate collapses; a rule repairs the estimate.

unit learn.seats
seats :: Int32 -> Int32

law seatsRule is
  definition:
    for all (rows :: Int32 where rows >= 0 && rows <= 40) => seats rows = rows * 4
    end for all

end law
end unit

hints: Run authored examples first. Which row counts are absent?
Add a named example for three rows; it should expect twelve seats.
Replace the branches with multiplication by four. Keep the property unchanged.

stages.title: Observe two passing examples
stages.action: Run examples. Predict seats 3, then add a third example to Tests. Run again.
stages.reason: Two familiar examples make the shortcut tempting. A new example checks whether the implementation follows the intended relationship.
stages.expect: The starter examples pass. A third-row example fails with the supplied implementation.
stages.recovery: Check that your new pair has a name and compares seats 3 with 12. F# array items are separated by newlines or semicolons.

stages.title: Introduce a general property
stages.action: Run all checks and read Contract.lawspec. Repair Solution, then run the same checks.
stages.reason: for all binds rows. The refinement limits the input domain to 0–40, avoiding overflow in this first exercise. The generated harness calls the implementation you edited.
stages.expect: The faulty function fails for a row count beyond the memorized cases. Multiplication by four passes.
stages.recovery: Read the first failing input and compare its result with four times the input. Do not weaken the rule to fit the faulty code.

stages.title: Try it independently
stages.action: Add examples for an empty hall and the largest stated hall. Explain why this is still scoped evidence. Mark your milestone after a passing run.
stages.reason: Boundary examples document intent; the general rule supplies checks between them.
stages.expect: 0 rows gives 0 seats; 40 rows gives 160. The milestone is separate from proof.
stages.recovery: If a boundary fails, check both the implementation and the expected value before editing the property.

lessons.title: A passing property can be too weak
lessons.slogan: Keep the items, not just their order.
lessons.vision: Sort a library waiting list without losing requests. You will learn to challenge a property with deliberately unhelpful implementations.
lessons.explanation: An F# list uses square brackets and semicolons: [3; 1; 1]. Empty brackets mean an empty list. The |> operator passes a value to the function on its right. List.pairwise forms neighboring pairs, and List.forall asks whether every pair satisfies the condition. With no pairs, that condition is true. && requires both conditions to hold. The expression fun (a, b) -> a <= b is an anonymous function: it names the two values in a pair and compares them. A comma groups the pair; a semicolon separates list items.
lessons.news: Ordering alone says nothing about keeping requests. Preservation must count duplicates as well as values: a set comparison alone can lose repeated requests.
lessons.contributions: A sorting implementation plus ordering and multiplicity preservation checks. You will reject empty output, a duplicate-dropping sort, and a same-length list of substituted values.

star.salient: Properties need to exclude plausible wrong behaviors.
star.slogan: Keep the items, not just their order.
star.symbol: The list-to-empty arrow displays an ordering pass beside a preservation failure.
star.surprise: Returning nothing passes every ordering check.
star.story: A waiting list looks perfectly sorted because every patron disappeared; preserving each request closes the loophole.

fsharp.Solution.fs:
module Solution

let sort (xs: int list) : int list = []
fsharp.Contract.lawspec:
-- ref:DEC-learn-course-preview
unit learn.sorting
sort :: List Int32 -> List Int32
function ordered (xs :: List Int32) -> Bool is
  first matching case of xs :
    when Nil then true
    when Cons h t then
      (first matching case of t :
        when Nil then true
        when Cons next rest then h <= next and ordered t
      end case)
  end case
end function

law sortingRule is
  definition:
    for all (xs :: List Int32) => ordered (sort xs) = true
    end for all
  end definition
end law
end unit

hints: There are no out-of-order pairs in an empty list.
Compare how often each value occurs before and after sorting. sameItems checks multiplicity.
List.sort preserves items. List.distinct intentionally removes duplicates and cannot repair a sorting function.

stages.title: A suspicious pass
stages.action: Run all checks with the empty-result implementation. Predict whether [3; 1; 1] is preserved.
stages.reason: No neighboring output pair violates ordering. The property has permitted an implementation that discards every request.
stages.expect: The ordering property passes; this is a real run of a weak property.
stages.recovery: Inspect sort in Solution. A passing result does not mean the waiting list was kept.

stages.title: Add preservation
stages.action: Load this stage to add sameItems to LawSpec and preservation to authored tests. Run, then repair sort.
stages.reason: sameItems requires each original value as many times in the result. It rejects lost duplicates and substituted values. A length check alone cannot do that.
stages.expect: The empty implementation fails. A correct sort passes both properties.
stages.recovery: Keep the original ordering condition. Preservation alone also permits an unchanged unsorted list.

stages.title: Challenge your property
stages.action: Try List.distinct followed by sorting, then a sorted list of zeros of the same length. Restore a correct implementation.
stages.reason: These mutants distinguish membership, multiplicity and length. Explain which property rejects each one.
stages.expect: Both mutants fail preservation; a correct sort is accepted, including duplicate values.
stages.recovery: Use [3; 1; 1] to inspect lost duplicates and [3; 1] to inspect substitutions. Run all checks after each edit.

lessons.title: Make a failure understandable
lessons.slogan: Find it large. Explain it small.
lessons.vision: Remove repeated ticket numbers while retaining ticket zero. You will improve a generator, shrink a failure, replay it and keep it as a regression example.
lessons.explanation: List.filter keeps only elements satisfying its function. fun x -> x <> 0 is an anonymous function: it returns true for anything except zero. List.distinct keeps the first occurrence of each value. A seed chooses a repeatable generated sequence. Shrinking tries smaller inputs after a failure; the path records the route to the final failing input.
lessons.news: A generator that never includes zero cannot reveal a zero-specific bug. Shrinking simplifies an observed failure; it does not search for every bug or guarantee a globally smallest input.
lessons.contributions: A generator including zero, a seeded run with a real shrink trace, a replay, a named regression example and repaired deduplication. The replay is meaningful only for the same code, property, generator and tool versions.

star.salient: Useful failures depend on both relevant generation and simplification.
star.slogan: Find it large. Explain it small.
star.symbol: The execution panel displays actual failed shrink candidates ending at [0].
star.surprise: Hundreds of positive ticket numbers miss the bug; a one-item list explains it.
star.story: A ticket import loses ticket zero. The learner widens the data, reduces the failure, records it and removes the accidental filter.

fsharp.Tests.fs:
module Tests
open Solution

let examples () : (string * bool) array =
    [| "repeated ticket", unique [2; 2; 3] = [2; 3] |]

let property (xs: int list) : bool =
    List.sort (unique xs) = List.sort (List.distinct xs)

let regressions : (string * bool) array = [||]
fsharp.Contract.lawspec:
-- ref:DEC-learn-course-preview
unit learn.unique
unique :: List Int32 -> List Int32

law uniqueRule is
  definition:
    for all (xs :: List Int32) => sameItems (unique xs) (toList (setOf xs))
    end for all
  end definition
end law
end unit

javascript.Solution.js: export function unique(xs) { return [...new Set(xs.filter(x => x !== 0))]; }

hints: Inspect generator.json. Does its minimum permit ticket zero?
Change min to -20 and rerun with seed 424242. Inspect the first failure and shrunk input.
Save the counterexample, replay it before editing, then remove the filter that drops zero.

stages.title: Notice the blind spot
stages.action: Run authored examples and the sampled property. Inspect generator.json. Predict unique [0].
stages.reason: The generator starts at 1. Passing samples cannot establish what happens to ticket zero. Run all checks also includes the independent LawSpec generator, which may reveal the blind spot sooner.
stages.expect: Authored samples pass. A direct zero example disagrees.
stages.recovery: Use Run sampled property to inspect this generator independently of LawSpec checks.

stages.title: Generate and shrink
stages.action: Load this stage to include zero and negative values. Run sampled property at seed 424242. Inspect the first failure, failed shrink candidates and final input. Replay before editing.
stages.reason: We expand the input domain before simplifying the failure. The seed/path belongs to the actual fast-check execution, not a simulated animation.
stages.expect: The supplied code fails and shrinks to [0]. Replay reaches the same counterexample.
stages.recovery: If you edited the generator, reset the seed and clear the replay path for a fresh run. A changed generator needs a fresh replay record.

stages.title: Save and repair
stages.action: Save the counterexample as a named example in Tests. Run examples to see it fail. Repair unique, then run examples and all checks.
stages.reason: The saved example makes this particular mistake easy to recognize later. Keep the general property to search beyond it.
stages.expect: The regression fails before repair. Removing the zero filter passes the same rerun.
stages.recovery: Save before repairing. In F#, [0] is a list of one integer; (=) checks its expected result.
